assignments.value: In this episode, I want to talk about something I think a lot of businesses get wrong when they start using AI, which is the assumption that the goal should be to automate as much as possible.  That sounds efficient on the surface. If AI can write, summarize, categorize, respond, organize, and make decisions faster than a person can, then it can be tempting to look at every manual task in the business and ask, “How do we automate this?”  But that is usually the wrong starting point.  The better question is: where does automation actually create leverage, and where does a human still need to stay involved?  Because not every repetitive task is a good automation candidate, and not every task that can technically be automated should be automated.  One of the clearest examples is content creation.  A business owner might look at the amount of time it takes to turn a podcast episode into a blog post and think, “AI can write a blog post, so let’s just automate the whole thing.”  And technically, yes, you can.  You can take a transcript, send it to a language model, generate a title, write the article, create metadata, generate schema, publish the post, create social media captions, schedule those posts, and do the entire thing without a person touching it.  But that does not automatically make it a good system.  If the model misunderstands the speaker’s point, invents a claim, uses the wrong tone, links to the wrong resource, or creates a blog post that technically looks fine but does not actually sound like the person or company, then the automation is doing more than saving time. It is also introducing risk.  That is why I think one of the most useful principles in AI implementation is to separate the parts of the workflow that require judgment from the parts that are deterministic.  If I am building a podcast-to-blog workflow, for example, I would absolutely use AI for the parts that require language understanding.  That might include identifying the main ideas in the transcript, reorganizing spoken language into a coherent written article, writing a meta description, generating FAQ content, and deciding which provided resources are actually relevant to the article.  Those are all tasks where context matters.  But I would not ask the model to do things that do not require judgment if I can handle them with predictable workflow logic instead.  If I already have a YouTube URL, I do not need the model to figure out how to create the embed code.  I can extract the video ID with JavaScript, validate it, and generate the iframe HTML deterministically.  That is more reliable.  The same thing applies to input validation.  If a transcript is missing, I do not want to spend money sending an empty request to an AI model and then hope the model figures out that something is wrong.  I want the workflow to stop before the API call.  If the YouTube URL is malformed, I want the workflow to catch that before the expensive part of the process begins.  And if the AI response comes back missing a required field, I do not want the workflow to continue creating documents as if everything is fine.  I want it to fail clearly.  That kind of design is not as flashy as saying that the whole workflow is autonomous, but it is usually much more useful.  And that brings me to another thing I think businesses misunderstand about AI automation: reliability matters more than novelty.  A system is valuable when someone can trust it.  If I build something that works perfectly in a demo but fails unpredictably when the inputs change, that is not a useful implementation.  It is a prototype.  There is nothing wrong with prototypes, but they should be treated as prototypes.  A production-quality automation has to account for things like bad input, missing input, unexpected responses, authentication failures, rate limits, and the fact that external services change.  Even a fairly simple workflow benefits from thinking through those things.  It also helps to be clear about where human review belongs.  I do not think human-in-the-loop workflows are a compromise.  In a lot of cases, they are the better design.  Take publishing content again.  The AI can do 80 or 90 percent of the transformation work.  It can take a long transcript and turn it into a structured article package in seconds.  That is a huge time savings.  But if the final output represents a person’s ideas, brand, expertise, or public reputation, it can still make sense for a person to review it before publication.  That does not mean the automation failed.  It means the automation removed the expensive, repetitive part of the process while preserving human judgment where it matters.  The same principle applies beyond content.  You might automate customer support triage without allowing the AI to issue refunds automatically.  You might automate lead qualification without allowing the system to send a contract without review.  You might automate reporting without allowing the AI to change financial data.  You might automate document drafting without allowing the system to send the final legal document directly to a client.  The goal is not to remove humans from the workflow.  The goal is to use humans where human judgment is most valuable.  Another thing I think is important is documentation.  AI workflows can become surprisingly difficult to understand if the logic only exists inside someone’s head.  A workflow might have several nodes, API calls, code transformations, validation steps, and authentication requirements.  If none of that is documented, the person who built it becomes the only person who can maintain it.  That is not a scalable system.  Good documentation should explain what the workflow does, what the inputs are, what each major step is responsible for, what credentials are required, what happens when something fails, and what parts of the workflow are intentionally manual.  It should also explain design decisions.  For example, if I use AI to generate content but JavaScript to create a YouTube embed, I want someone reviewing the system to understand why.  It is not because the AI could not generate the embed.  It is because deterministic logic is the better tool for that part of the problem.  That distinction matters.  One of the things I like about AI implementation work is that the challenge is usually not just getting the model to produce an answer.  The interesting part is designing the system around the model.  What information should the model receive?  What should be validated before the request?  What format should the response use?  What happens if the response is incomplete?  What should be handled with code instead?  Where should a person review the result?  How do you prevent credentials from ending up in a public repository?  How do you make the workflow understandable to someone who did not build it?  Those are implementation questions, not just prompting questions.  And I think that is where a lot of businesses are going to need help.  They do not necessarily need someone to show them another clever ChatGPT prompt.  They need someone who can look at an existing business process, identify where AI is actually useful, connect the systems, put safeguards around the model, test the workflow, document it, and make sure the result solves the original problem.  That is a very different skill set from simply knowing how to use an AI chatbot.  It requires some understanding of process design.  It requires technical curiosity.  It requires being comfortable with APIs and automation tools.  And it requires enough judgment to know when not to use AI.  That last part is probably one of the most important.  If a simple rule can solve the problem more reliably, use the rule.  If JavaScript can transform the data predictably, use JavaScript.  If an IF condition can reject bad input before an API call, use the IF condition.  Use the language model for the parts where language, ambiguity, context, or judgment are actually involved.  That usually produces a system that is cheaper, easier to test, easier to explain, and easier to maintain.  So if you are looking at a business process and trying to figure out whether it should be automated, I would start with three questions.  First, where is the repetitive work?  Second, which parts of that work require real judgment?  And third, what would happen if the automation got something wrong?  Those three questions will usually tell you a lot.  If the work is repetitive, low-risk, and governed by clear rules, that is often a strong automation candidate.  If the work is repetitive but requires interpretation, that may be a good place to use AI with validation.  And if the consequences of a mistake are significant, that is where you probably want human review.  That is a much better framework than simply asking, “Can AI do this?”  Because in 2026, the answer to that question is very often yes.  The more useful question is whether AI should do it, and if so, what the surrounding system needs to look like to make that automation reliable.

values.content:
=Transform the podcast transcript below into a publication-ready blog content package.

Return exactly these fields:

- blog_title
- meta_title
- meta_description
- html
- faq_schema

Requirements:

- blog_title: Clear, compelling title for the article.
- meta_title: SEO-friendly title suitable for search results.
- meta_description: Concise search description.
- html: The complete blog post as clean HTML. Do not wrap it in Markdown code fences.
- faq_schema: Valid FAQPage JSON-LD as a string. Do not wrap it in Markdown code fences.

Use only information supported by the transcript.
Do not invent facts, statistics, quotes, claims, URLs, products, or resources.

Relevant resources:

{{$json.relevant_links}}

When one or more of these resources are genuinely relevant to the article, include them naturally within the HTML using descriptive anchor text.

Do not force a resource into the article if it is not relevant.
Use only URLs provided in the Relevant resources section above.

Writing style requirements:

- Preserve the speaker's natural voice, point of view, and level of directness.
- Keep the writing conversational rather than turning it into generic corporate or editorial prose.
- Use natural contractions where appropriate.
- Do not use em dashes. Use commas, periods, colons, or parentheses instead.
- Avoid generic AI-style transitions and overly polished business language.
- Do not introduce terminology or phrasing that is more formal than the source unless needed for clarity.
- Improve organization and readability without flattening the speaker's personality.

Podcast transcript:

{{$json.transcript}}
